We report millimeter/submillimeter continuum and molecular line observations of the Galactic super star cluster RCW 38, obtained from the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array with a minimum angular resolution of $0''17\times0''15$ ($\simeq289\,{\rm AU}\times255\,{\rm AU}$).

In order to acquire better sensitivities, a uv-tapering was applied to the $^{12}$CO and C$^{18}$O$_{\rm all}$ data, which resulted in larger synthesized beams of $\sim$0$''.$5 and $\sim$2$''$, respectively.

The ALMA observations in RCW 38 (P.I.: Fukui, Y., #2015.1.01134.S) were conducted for the central 1.5 pc $\times$ 0.7 pc of IRS 1 and IRS 2 in the ALMA band-6 and band-7, using the main 12-m array and the Atacama Compact Array (ACA).

findings_qualitative.value: Twenty-one massive, gravitationally bound C18O condensations are embedded within 0.1-0.2 pc wide filamentary structures extending northwest-southeast in the center of RCW 38, and all except #13 (harboring Source A) lack compact 233-GHz continuum sources and are likely starless precursors of intermediate- or high-mass stars.

evidence.quote: The virial parameter, $\alpha_{\rm vir}$ = $M_{\rm vir}$/$M_{\rm H_2}$, is the order of unity, suggesting that these condensations are gravitationally bounded.

evidence.loc: Formation of massive condensations in RCW 38
evidence.quote: The observed core properties, especially mass and size, in RCW 38 are consistent with those in infrared dark clouds on the Galactic plane (e.g., (cite: oha2016)), indicating that the identified condensations are likely precursors of high-mass or at least intermediate-mass stars.

findings_qualitative.value: The eastern rim of C18O condensation #13 follows the western rim of IRS 1, while IRS 1 coincides with H30alpha emission, indicating IRS 1 arises from strong irradiation of the outer envelope of condensation #13 by IRS 2.

evidence.quote: indicating that the eastern rim of the condensation #13 follows the western rim of the bright ridge of IRS 1, and IRS 1 is spatially coincident with the H30$\alpha_{\rm ACA}$ distribution. This result suggests that the bright infrared emission of IRS 2 arises from the strong irradiation of the outer envelope of the condensation by the adjacent IRS 2.

findings_qualitative.value: Both Source A and Source B show single continuum peaks at 270 AU resolution with no signs of fragmentation and no H30alpha or infrared excess, indicating deeply embedded massive protostars prior to ionizing their surroundings.

evidence.loc: Discovery of two compact mm-sources: Source A and Source B
evidence.quote: This nature is consistent with the non-detection of H30$\alpha$ emission from the continuum peaks with the 12-m array, meaning that the young sources do not start to ionize their surroundings.

evidence.loc: Source A and Source B; nurseries of massive protostars?
evidence.quote: Note that the two sources exhibit a single peak at the 270 AU resolution, indicating no signs of fragmentation.

claims.hypothesis: Source A and Source B harbor massive protostars in a very early evolutionary stage.
claims.experiment: High-resolution ALMA 233-GHz and 341-GHz_ACA continuum imaging and 12CO J=2-1 outflow mapping of RCW 38.
claims.result: Two compact dust sources (radii ~460 and ~200 AU) embedded in massive cores (16-81 M_sun) drive high-velocity (30-70 km/s) 12CO outflows with short dynamical timescales (<1000 yr), high mass outflow rates (10^-4 to 10^-3 M_sun yr^-1), and mechanical forces of ~10^-2 M_sun km s^-1 yr^-1.
claims.finding: The dense core masses, high outflow forces, high inferred mass accretion rates, and short dynamical timescales indicate that Source A and Source B harbor massive protostars in an early creation stage.

evidence.loc: Source A and Source B; nurseries of massive protostars?
evidence.quote: These observational signatures imply that Source A and Source B harbor massive protostars that can drive energetic outflows.
The short dynamical timescales of the outflows, less than 1000 yr, suggest that the protostars in Source A and Source B may be massive stars in the creation stage.

claims.hypothesis: The velocity gradient of C18O J=2-1 emission around Source A traces a Keplerian rotating protostellar disk.
claims.experiment: First-moment and position-velocity diagram analysis of high-resolution C18O J=2-1 emission toward Source A and comparison with the 12CO outflow axis.
claims.result: A velocity gradient of ~2 km s^-1 is observed across the central 2000 AU of Source A, but the C18O distribution does not perfectly coincide with the 233-GHz peak and the outflow lobes are not perpendicular to the velocity gradient.
claims.finding: The velocity gradient could be interpreted as Keplerian rotation around a few M_sun object or as infall motion, and there is no robust evidence that the C18O component directly traces a Keplerian disk.

evidence.loc: Velocity distribution of the C$^{18}$O emission in Source A
evidence.quote: However, the directions of the outflow lobes which will be presented in the next subsection are not perpendicular to the direction of the velocity gradient (see arrows in Figure 4(b)). This is inconsistent with the hypothesis that the observed C$^{18}$O component is a protostellar disk.

The high-resolution C$^{18}$O image shows a velocity gradient of gas toward Source A, which can be interpreted as the rotation, although there is no robust evidence for directly tracing the Keplerian motion of Source A.

claims.hypothesis: The infrared-quiet nature of Source A and Source B despite high inferred accretion rates is explained by extreme dust extinction or episodic accretion.
claims.experiment: Measured upper limits of 3.6-8.0 um luminosity from Spitzer/IRAC images and compared them with theoretical accretion luminosities derived from outflow mass-loss rates and dust optical depth estimates.
claims.result: L_3.6-8.0 upper limits are 3.0 L_sun (Source A) and 1.6 L_sun (Source B), two orders of magnitude below predicted L_acc (140-1700 L_sun), while column densities N_H2 > 10^24 cm^-2 imply 3.6-8.0 um optical depths of 50-100.
claims.finding: Both high dust extinction by the dense envelopes and quiescent phases in an episodic accretion scenario are viable explanations for the lack of near- and mid-infrared emission.

evidence.quote: Even for a small $M_{*}$ of 0.1 $M_\odot$, the derived $L_{\rm acc}$ is approximately two order of magnitude larger than the derived upper-limits of $L_{3.6-8.0}$ for Source A and Source B.

One idea is attenuation of the emission by dust in Source A and Source B. Another idea is the episodic accretion scenario, in which protostars spend most of their time in the quiescent phase, interspersed with short accretion bursts.

claims.hypothesis: The filamentary structures and massive C18O condensations in RCW 38 were formed via the collect-and-collapse process driven by feedback from the central O stars (IRS 2).
claims.experiment: Compared the spatial separation between IRS 2 and the condensations (~0.3 pc) with the filament width (0.1-0.2 pc) and required gas compression factor.
claims.result: Because the distance to IRS 2 (~0.3 pc) is comparable to the filament width, plane-parallel accumulation can only increase gas density by a factor of ~2 rather than the 1-2 orders of magnitude required for collect-and-collapse fragmentation.
claims.finding: Collect-and-collapse compression by adjacent O-star feedback is eliminated as the origin of the condensations; instead, they were likely formed prior to ionization, possibly triggered by a cloud-cloud collision.

evidence.loc: Formation of massive condensations in RCW 38
evidence.quote: In the case of RCW 38, however, the distance between the massive condensations and exciting source (IRS 2) is too small for the accumulated gas to induce fragmentation.

We discussed the formation scenario of the filamentary structures and massive condensations in RCW 38, and eliminated the possibility of gas compression by the feedback from nearby O stars. A collision between two molecular clouds may have triggered the formation of the filamentary structures in which the massive condensations were formed.

why_this_data.value: RCW 38 is the youngest super star cluster in the Milky Way (0.1-0.5 Myr) at 1.7 kpc with abundant remaining molecular gas in its central ~1 pc, and ALMA Cycle 3 Band 6 and 7 observations provide the ~270 AU resolution needed to resolve fragmentation, collapse, and outflows in massive YSOs.

evidence.quote: Despite strong dissipative and destructive effects caused by feedback from the formed massive stars, plenty of molecular gas still remains within the central $\sim$1 pc of RCW 38, offering a unique opportunity to observe the natal gas of the super star cluster during formation (cite: fuk2016).
The minimum angular resolution of the dataset is $0''.17\times0''.15$, which corresponds to 289$\times$255 AU at 1.7 kpc.

why_this_method.value: Used 341-GHz_ACA rather than 233-GHz_ACA for core mass estimates because 233-GHz_ACA is contaminated by free-free emission; adopted a CO-to-H2 conversion factor for outflow masses because low S/N in 12-m line data prevents disentangling opacity and excitation effects.
